title: Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 2.2 Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables
intro: After this lesson you can compute marginal, joint and conditional relative frequencies from a two-way table, write them in $P(\ )$ notation, and use them to justify a claim about association.

moments.title: Marginal relative frequency
moments.text: A row or column total divided by the table total. Only one category is named.

moments.title: $P(\ )$ notation
moments.text: Put what you are looking for in the parentheses. It is notation, not multiplication.

moments.title: Bus riders, walkers and tardy students
moments.text: $35/188\approx0.186$ rode the bus, $34/188\approx0.181$ walked, and $64/188\approx0.340$ were tardy.

moments.title: Joint relative frequency
moments.text: A cell count divided by the table total. The question joins two categories with "and".

moments.title: Conditional relative frequency
moments.text: A cell divided by the total of its row or column. The condition restricts who you look at.

moments.title: The condition can be anywhere in the sentence
moments.text: In notation the condition always goes after the vertical bar.

moments.title: The condition sets the denominator
moments.text: $9/35\approx0.257$ of bus riders were tardy. The denominator is 35, not 188.

moments.title: Association from proportions
moments.text: Adding a condition changes the proportion when two variables are associated.

moments.title: Transport and tardiness
moments.text: 34.0% overall, but 25.7% of bus riders and 45.6% of self-drivers were tardy.

moments.title: Write the conclusion in context
moments.text: Answer the question, give the baseline, then compare the conditional proportions.

moments.title: Expected cell count with no association
moments.text: If there were no association, 34% of the 90 self-drivers, about 31, would be tardy.

moments.title: Fitness tracker and fitness level
moments.text: A mix of marginal, joint and conditional questions on 162 adults.

moments.title: Tracker use differs by fitness level
moments.text: About 67% overall, 60% of the high-fitness group and 78% of the low-fitness group wear a tracker, so there is an association.

moments.title: Wart treatment at two clinics
moments.text: About 59% overall, 63% at clinic A and 52% at clinic B had success.

cards.name: Marginal
cards.text: One category named. Divide a total from the margin by the table total.

cards.name: Joint
cards.text: Two categories joined by "and". Divide one cell by the table total.

cards.name: Conditional
cards.text: "Of those who", "given that" or "among". Divide by the total of the condition.

cells: What proportion of students rode the bus?
What proportion rode the bus and were tardy?
Of those who rode the bus, what proportion were tardy?
What proportion of tardy students drove themselves?
What proportion were tardy, given that they walked?
What proportion walked and were not tardy?

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The condition can appear at the start, middle or end of the question. Find the group you are told to restrict to; that group total is the denominator.

sections.title: Justify an association claim
sections.intro: Start with a baseline, then add a condition and see whether the proportion changes. If it does, the variables are associated.
steps: Find the marginal proportion for the outcome. This is the baseline.
Find the outcome proportion within each group, with the group total as the denominator.
Compare each conditional proportion to the baseline and to each other.
Write the conclusion in context: say there is an association, quote the numbers, and describe the direction.

parts.label: No association
parts.text: Expected tardy self-drivers if the rate stayed the same.

traps.title: Dividing by the table total for a conditional
traps.better: $9/35\approx0.257$ of bus riders were tardy. The condition "bus riders" sets the denominator.

traps.title: Reversing the condition
traps.weak: Of those who wear a tracker, 60.7% have high fitness.

traps.title: Association stated without numbers
traps.weak: Yes, there is an association between clinic and success.
traps.better: Yes, there is an association between clinic and success. Overall about 59% had success, but about 63% at clinic A and 52% at clinic B did.

traps.title: Comparing counts
traps.weak: More patients at clinic A had success (88 against 35), so A is better.
traps.better: Clinic A treated more patients. Compare proportions: $88/139\approx0.633$ and $35/68\approx0.515$.

traps.title: Explaining why
traps.weak: Clinic A works better because its doctors are more skilled.
traps.better: The data show an association in this sample. The statistics do not explain why.

questions.stem: A survey of 120 students has 80 in Grade 9 and 40 in Grade 10. In all, 48 Grade 9 students and 12 Grade 10 students buy cafeteria lunch. What is the joint relative frequency of Grade 10 and cafeteria lunch?
why: This is the conditional proportion of Grade 10 students who buy cafeteria lunch, not the joint.
Correct. A joint relative frequency divides the cell count by the table total: $12/120=0.10$.
60 is the cafeteria total, so this is the proportion of cafeteria buyers who are in Grade 10, a conditional proportion.
This is the marginal proportion buying cafeteria lunch.

questions.stem: Using the same survey, which expression gives the proportion of cafeteria buyers who are in Grade 9?
why: This is the share of Grade 9 students who buy cafeteria lunch, with the condition reversed.
This is the joint relative frequency.
Correct. The condition is cafeteria buyers, so the denominator is the cafeteria total of 60: $48/60=0.80$.
This is the marginal proportion buying cafeteria lunch.

questions.stem: Overall 50% of the 120 students buy cafeteria lunch. If lunch choice and grade were not associated, how many of the 80 Grade 9 students would buy cafeteria lunch?
why: Correct. With no association the Grade 9 rate matches the overall rate: $0.50\times80=40$.
This is the observed count for Grade 9. It exceeds 40, which is why the variables are associated.
This is the total number of cafeteria buyers in both grades.
30 would be half of the 60 cafeteria buyers, which does not use the Grade 9 group size.

questions.stem: Which statement best justifies the claim that grade and lunch choice are associated?
opts: More Grade 9 students than Grade 10 students buy cafeteria lunch.
60% of Grade 9 students but 30% of Grade 10 students buy cafeteria lunch.
why: The number of cells says nothing about the variables.
A large overall count does not compare groups.
This compares counts, but Grade 9 is also twice as large. The justification needs proportions.
Correct. The conditional proportions differ across grades, which is evidence of association.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A school asked 150 students whether they use a paper planner or a phone app to manage homework. Among 80 ninth graders, 52 use the app. Among 70 eleventh graders, 21 use the app.
parts: (a) Complete a two-way table with totals.
(b) What proportion of all students use the app? Is this a marginal, joint or conditional proportion?
(c) What proportion of app users are eleventh graders? Write it in $P(\ )$ notation.
(d) Is there an association between grade and planner type? Justify with summary statistics.
sample: (a) Ninth: 52 app, 28 paper, total 80. Eleventh: 21 app, 49 paper, total 70. Column totals: 73 app, 77 paper, total 150.
(b) $73/150=0.487$. This is marginal because only one category is named.

(d) Yes, there is an association between grade and planner type. Overall about 49% use the app, but 65% of ninth graders and 30% of eleventh graders do. The proportions differ, so grade and planner type are associated in this sample.
checklist: (d) Baseline and both conditional proportions in context
